extracted.intended_audience: writers/authors seeking literary representation and traditional publication
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on when you need an agent, how to research and approach agents, what materials to submit, and how to evaluate and choose the best agent for your book and career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do you need a literary agent?
rubrics_metrics.description: It depends on what you’re selling. If you want to be published by one of the major New York houses ... then you more or less need to have one—and want one on your side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents are essential if targeting Big Five publishers (Penguin Random House, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, Macmillan). For niche markets, academic, or some literary works, you might not need an agent. Agents are motivated by the size of the advance they expect to get; if your project won’t command a decent advance, you may need to sell the project on your own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial viability / suitability for New York houses
rubrics_metrics.description: There are different levels of commercial viability: some books are “big” books, suitable for Big Five traditional publishers, while others are “quiet” books, suitable for mid-size and small presses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genres commonly suitable for Big Five: genre or mainstream fiction (romance, erotica, mystery/crime, thriller, science fiction, fantasy, young adult, new adult). Nonfiction must have a strong hook or concept and an author platform; NY publishers usually won’t sign nonfiction unless it anticipates selling 10,000 to 20,000 copies minimum. Be honest about your work’s potential and target publishers accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research agents using industry resources
rubrics_metrics.description: PublishersMarketplace.com is the best place to research literary agents; you can search the publishing deals database by genre, category, and/or keyword to pinpoint the best agents for your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other resources: QueryTracker (free/paid) and Duotrope. Check the Twitter hashtag #MSWL and the Manuscript Wish List site (official and unofficial aggregators) to see what agents/editors are actively seeking. Study deals announced to learn what commercial publishing looks like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish and polish your manuscript/proposal before submitting
rubrics_metrics.description: You should finish (and polish) your manuscript or book proposal before submitting. One of the biggest mistakes new writers make is rushing to get published when there’s no reason to rush.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect the agent to help you to the finish line on your manuscript. While some agents may do editorial work, you'll get a much better response if you submit work you can see no further way to improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know what materials agents commonly request
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common materials you’ll be asked for: Query letter; Novel synopsis; Nonfiction book proposal; Novel proposal; Sample chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Query letter: one-page pitch describing your work. Novel synopsis: brief summary (usually no more than one or two pages) of your story, from beginning to end, and must reveal the ending. Nonfiction book proposal: complex, usually 20–30 pages (minimum). Novel proposal: often includes a query letter, a synopsis, and perhaps the first chapter. Sample chapters: for fiction, start at the beginning of the manuscript; for nonfiction any chapter is usually acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow agents' submission guidelines; expect queries not fulls
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost no agent accepts full manuscripts on first contact. This is what “no unsolicited materials” means when you read submission guidelines. Almost all agents will accept a one-page query letter unless their guidelines state otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agent's guidelines state they do not accept queries, they are closed. Send precisely what the agent requests; do not send unsolicited fulls unless asked.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to interpret agent responses
rubrics_metrics.description: After you send out queries, you’ll get a mix of responses: no response at all (which means rejection); a request for a partial manuscript and possibly a synopsis; a request for the full manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you receive no requests for the manuscript or book proposal, there might be something wrong with your query. If you get requests but later rejections, there may be a weakness in the manuscript or proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent sales track record
rubrics_metrics.description: What’s her sales track record? This is usually the number-one sign of whether you have a good agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate client list and the publishers the agent has recently sold to. Are they appropriate for your work? Are the advances her clients command in the 'good' range for you? Find deals reported at PublishersMarketplace (subscription required) or agent websites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider new agents vs established agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes it’s easier to get represented by a new agent who is trying to build a roster of clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new and 'hungry' agent can work out well for a new author with a potentially small deal. If an agent’s track record is developing, check prior experience (e.g., former editor) and the agency's reputation. Beware if someone has been trying to develop their list for a very long time without traction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent communication and professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Does her communication inspire confidence? Timeless signs of professionalism: they get back to you in a timely manner, communicate clearly and respectfully, and their business operations aren’t cloaked in secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good agent will not leave clients in the dark for extended periods and will offer clarity about each stage of the process. However, don’t expect immediate/constant contact—agents prioritize established revenue-generating clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent enthusiasm and fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you get the feeling that the agent genuinely believes in you and your work? Enthusiasm matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enthusiasm indicates the agent will champion your cause to publishers and be invested in your long-term career. Chemistry between agent and author is often as important as raw track record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent involvement in feedback and repositioning
rubrics_metrics.description: A good agent will have a conversation with you about any rejections received and share meaningful feedback from editors/publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agent should discuss how your book or proposal could be repositioned to sell or explain if the project would take far more work than is worth his time. You have a right to know what publishers were queried and to discuss repositioning strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent should improve your query/proposal package
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the agent help you improve your query, pitch, and/or proposal? A good agent will improve the query/proposal package.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents typically provide at least one round of feedback and revision to ensure the pitch or proposal is primed for success; few authors produce a perfect proposal without agent input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent knowledge of contracts and negotiation skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Your agent MUST know his way around a book contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good agent understands where to ask for more money or rights, knows if a client is getting the best deal possible, and will revise boilerplate contract language. If an agent passes you a publisher’s boilerplate contract with no changes, that’s a red flag. Agents also advise on non-monetary pros/cons of offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent as long-term business manager and advocate
rubrics_metrics.description: A great agent is an author’s business manager, mentor, and cheerleader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents should hold your hand when things go wrong with an editor or publisher, celebrate successes, look for opportunities, attend to financial interests, and support big-picture career growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation and industry recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: People in the industry should recognize the name of your agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can’t find any online mention of your agent and he’s not a member of the Association of American Literary Agents (AALA), that’s a red flag. Check recent sales and affiliations; agency size alone doesn’t necessarily correlate with agent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard agent compensation and fee warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally, agents get paid only when they sell your work, and they receive a 15 percent commission on everything you get paid (your advance and royalties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is best to avoid agents who charge fees other than the standard 15 percent. Beware of agents who add third parties that reduce your earnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch out for amateur or unethical agents
rubrics_metrics.description: For more excellent information on how to tell a good agent from a not-so-good agent, check out Writer Beware on Literary Agents (or go straight to the section on Amateur Agents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use watchdog resources to screen for amateur agents and scams. Check credentials, track record, and community reputation before signing.

rubrics_metrics.name: If not suitable for NY houses, pursue alternative publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: If your work doesn’t look like a good candidate for a New York house, don’t despair. There are many mid-size houses, independent publishers, small presses, university presses, regional presses, and digital-only publishers who might be thrilled to have your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust your submissions and agent expectations to target publishers that match your book’s commercial profile; you just need to find them and research appropriate lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use market data to learn what sells
rubrics_metrics.description: To better understand what sells, buy a month-long subscription to PublishersMarketplace.com and study the deals that get announced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying deal announcements provides a quick education in commercial publishing and helps you see which agents and editors are active in your genre.
